headline: Skip the boat ramp line — the blues are stacked right off the beach at Jones
subhead: Everybody's booking fluke charters for the bay while bunker schools get shredded to pieces thirty yards off the sand.
body_markdown:
I had a guy at the bait shop this morning tell me he was heading out to drift Sloop Channel for fluke and I just about spit my coffee. Not because fluke's bad right now — it's fine, we'll get to it — but because he was driving right past the best fishing on this whole stretch of coast to go sit in a boat in the heat. The bluefish blitz is happening right now, right off the beach, and half the guys around here are still treating it like a footnote.

I said it last week and I'll say it again — this bunker-bluefish thing isn't slowing down, it's spreading. We flagged this pattern building and here it is in full swing: bunker schools are getting pinned against the jetty rocks at Jones Inlet on the last two hours of the outgoing tide, and the blues are just wrecking them. I watched it happen three mornings this week from the rocks at the west end near the Coast Guard station — bait skying out of the water, birds diving, blues cutting through pods so hard you can hear it from fifty yards off. That's not subtle fishing. That's just showing up and not messing it up.

Tactics are dead simple right now and that's the beauty of it. I'm throwing a 2-ounce Hopkins Shorty or a bunker-colored Ava jig, no wire needed if you're not afraid of losing a few bucktails to bluefish teeth — but if you want to keep your gear, tie on 30 pounds of fluorocarbon leader minimum, because these fish are 4 to 10 pounds and they're not shy about biting through mono. Bombers and topwater poppers are also getting hit hard when the blitz comes up shallow, which it's been doing right around the last hour of the outgoing when bait gets squeezed against the rocks with nowhere to go. That's your window. Don't sleep past 6:30 AM out there — once the sun gets up and the tide slacks, the whole thing goes quiet until the next push.

Now for the bass — and I'll be straight with you, daytime striper fishing off the surf right now is basically dead. Water's pushed into the mid-70s along the beachfront and these fish know better than to sit in that soup during daylight. They've gone nocturnal on us, which means if you want stripers you're fishing dawn, dusk, or full dark. I've been working the Short Beach jetties right at first light, drifting live bunker on a fish-finder rig in maybe 12 to 15 feet right off the rocks, and picking up a few schoolies and the occasional slot fish in that 28 to 32 inch range. Nothing to write home about volume-wise, but it's honest work and it beats fishing empty water at noon. If you want a real shot at a bigger bass, fish the two hours around the bottom of the tide change at night with a bunker chunk sitting on the bottom in the deeper cuts off the inlet — that's where the bigger fish have been holding, out of the warm surface layer.

Fluke's steady, not spectacular. The drift through Sloop Channel and out toward the deeper water off Jones Inlet is still producing, but you've got to work for keepers. Shorts are everywhere — I mean everywhere, you'll go through two dozen before you find one that measures. The better fish, the 20-inch-plus stuff, are sitting in that deeper channel water, 25 to 35 feet, and they want the stronger tide stages. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow right along the bottom on the meat of the incoming or outgoing — that's been my producer. Don't bother drifting the shallow flats in the middle of the day right now, the water's too warm and the good fish have moved off it.

Weakfish are a genuine bright spot if you know where to look. I've been picking a few up in the deeper holes around the Wantagh Bridge pilings on the last of the outgoing, fishing bucktails tipped with a strip of squid, working it slow near bottom. Nothing like the old days but there's real life there this summer, more than I've seen in a few years, and if that pattern keeps building the way it has, this could turn into something worth chasing seriously by August.

Blackfish and porgies are basically off the table until the water cools — not worth your gas right now.

Looking ahead, I don't see any reason for the bluefish blitz to quit. Bunker are still thick along this beach and the weather's calm and stable, which is exactly the recipe that keeps bait pinned tight and blues fed. If the wind stays out of the south and light like it has been, I'd fish that same outgoing window at Jones Inlet again this weekend — same spot, same tide, same jigs. If a stiff northeast blow comes through and scatters the bunker, that could shut it down fast, so get out there while it's good instead of waiting for someone to tell you it's still going. For bass, keep it dark and keep it patient — that's the program until this heat breaks.
